questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why some everyday sounds make people very upset
How to stop biting your nails
How loud noise can slowly damage our hearing over time
questions.why: They find out about misophonia, where everyday sounds make people angry or upset.

questions.q: What is the awful noise Neil hears at the start?
questions.why: Phil apologises: “I was, er… biting my nails.”

questions.q: According to some estimates, how many people are emotionally affected by sounds others make?
questions.why: Neil says one person in five is affected emotionally by these sounds.

questions.q: What kind of sounds often trigger misophonia?
options: Sounds linked to food and eating
Birds and animals outside the house
questions.why: Neil says the triggers often involve food and eating, so family dinners can feel like torture.

questions.q: What response do certain sounds cause in Olana Tansley-Hancock?
options: She loses her hearing for a short while after the noise stops
A sudden fight-or-flight reaction she can't control
questions.why: She describes a fight-or-flight response – an immediate, uncontrollable reaction.

questions.q: Why does Olana mention being chased by wild animals?
options: She was once attacked by an animal
To show her reaction to harmless sounds is unusual
To explain what first caused her misophonia as a child
questions.why: She says we rarely face such dangers today, yet she feels that response to innocuous sounds.

questions.q: What does Olana compare her reaction to?
options: Hearing that someone close to you has died
Being very tired after a long, busy day at work
questions.why: She says the immediacy is like when someone tells you a person close to you has passed away.

questions.q: Which trick does Phil say helps people with misophonia?
options: Wearing earplugs all day, even while she is asleep
Background music and explaining the condition
questions.why: He says background music can disguise eating sounds, and explaining the condition helps.
